title: Colors That Stop Matching
tagline: Two paints match in the shop, then clash under the lamps at home. Here is why.
description: An interactive lesson on why two paints that match under one lamp can clash under another, an effect called metamerism. Switch lamps, wiggle a paint's curve without changing its color, make your own matching pair and try lamps from a shop light to a sodium street lamp. Every color is computed in your browser from the international standard tables for light and color vision.
intro: An interactive lesson on why two paints that match under one lamp can clash under another, for anyone who has chosen paint or matched socks. Change the lamp over Pebble and Fog, then wiggle Fog's curve (the share of each color of light it sends back): its color will not budge.

makingOf: This page is an Opus cameo: it was built by a team of Claude Opus agents instead of the usual Sonnet team. Every color on it is computed in your browser from CIE tables: the 1931 standard observer and the CIE illuminants A, D65, FL11 and LED-B2. The sodium street lamp (one line at 589 nm), the smooth 3999 K glow and the screen's three color bands are modeled, and the page says so wherever they appear. Pebble and Fog were designed by a script that searched for the smoothest pair of curves that match exactly under the shop light for the CIE's 1931 and 1964 standard observers and its 2015 cone-based observer alike, and split by about 19 under the warm bulb, with a change in lightness and in yellow against blue, so that the split also shows for most color-blind visitors. Color differences use CIEDE2000, checked against the 34 published test pairs of Sharma, Wu and Dalal; the page re-checks its numbers each time it loads.
